title: Extension Ladder Fall Prevention
summary: Most ladder falls in construction involve extension ladders that slip, shift, or throw the worker off balance. This talk covers inspection, the 4-to-1 angle, tie-offs, and the 3-foot extension.
talking_points: When you can, use an aerial lift or scaffold instead of a ladder for work at height.
Inspect the rails, rungs, feet, and rung locks or spreaders every time you use the ladder. Tag any damaged ladder 'do not use' and get another.
Check the ladder's duty rating so it holds you plus your tools and tool belt.

Set the ladder on a solid, stable base at a 4-to-1 angle: for every 4 feet of working height, move the base 1 foot out. Check it by standing on the feet with your arms straight out - your palms should just reach a rung.
Screw a 2-by-4 cleat to the ground behind the feet to stop it sliding back. Tie off the top, and the bottom if possible, to stop it sliding sideways.
Extend the ladder 3 feet above the landing. Use both hands when climbing up and down.
site_hazards_to_check: Damaged rails, rungs, feet, or rung locks, or a ladder over or under its duty rating
Ladder set steeper or flatter than the 4-to-1 angle
Soft, uneven, or slippery base with no cleat behind the feet
Ladder top not tied off, or resting less than 3 feet above the landing
Ladder used where a lift or scaffold would be safer
discussion_questions: How do you set and check the 4-to-1 angle on this ladder?
How is the ladder secured top and bottom so it cannot slip?
How far above the landing should the ladder rails stick up?
